content: 1. Niacin extended-release is a medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. It is also indicated for the regression of atherosclerotic disease in patients with a history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and hyperlipidemia. Additionally, it is used as an adjunct to diet to reduce elevated total cholesterol (TC) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in adult patients with primary hyperlipidemia, and to lower triglycerides (TG) in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia. 2. Common adverse reactions associated with niacin extended-release include flushing, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, increased cough, and pruritus (itching). 3. Niacin therapy should be part of a comprehensive risk factor intervention strategy for individuals at significantly increased risk for atherosclerotic vascular disease due to hyperlipidemia. 4. NIASPAN, a brand of niacin extended-release, is specifically indicated to reduce elevated TC, LDL-C, Apo B, and TG levels, and to increase high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) in patients with primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. 5. NIASPAN, in combination with simvastatin or lovastatin, is indicated for the treatment of primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia when monotherapy with NIASPAN, simvastatin, or lovastatin is inadequate. 6. In patients with a history of myocardial infarction (MI) and hyperlipidemia, niacin is indicated to reduce the risk of recurrent nonfatal myocardial infarction. 7. In patients with a history of CAD and hyperlipidemia, niacin, in combination with a bile acid-binding resin, is indicated to reduce elevated TC and LDL-C levels in adult patients with primary hyperlipidemia. 8. Niacin is also indicated as adjunctive therapy for the treatment of adult patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia who are at risk of pancreatitis and do not respond adequately to dietary efforts. 9. NIASPAN should be taken at bedtime after a low-fat snack, and doses should be individualized based on patient response. Therapy should be initiated at 500 mg at bedtime to minimize the incidence and severity of side effects during early treatment. 10. The recommended maintenance dose of NIASPAN is 1,000 mg to 2,000 mg once daily at bedtime. Doses greater than 2,000 mg daily are not recommended. 11. Women may respond to lower doses of NIASPAN compared to men. Single-dose bioavailability studies have shown that two 500 mg tablets and one 1,000 mg tablet are interchangeable, but three 500 mg tablets and two 750 mg tablets are not. 12. If lipid response to NIASPAN alone is insufficient or if higher doses are not well tolerated, combination therapy with a bile acid-binding resin or statin may be beneficial. 13. Flushing of the skin, a common side effect, may be reduced in frequency or severity by pretreatment with aspirin (up to 325 mg taken 30 minutes prior to the NIASPAN dose). Tolerance to flushing typically develops over several weeks. 14. Flushing, pruritus, and gastrointestinal distress can also be minimized by gradually increasing the niacin dose and avoiding administration on an empty stomach. Concomitant consumption of alcohol, hot drinks, or spicy foods may exacerbate flushing and pruritus and should be avoided around the time of NIASPAN ingestion. 15. Equivalent doses of NIASPAN should not be substituted for sustained-release (modified-release, timed-release) niacin preparations or immediate-release (crystalline) niacin. 16. Patients previously receiving other niacin products should start with the recommended NIASPAN titration schedule, and the dose should be individualized based on patient response. 17. If NIASPAN therapy is discontinued for an extended period, reinitiation of therapy should include a titration phase. 18. NIASPAN tablets should be taken whole and should not be broken, crushed, or chewed before swallowing. 19. Caution should be exercised when using NIASPAN in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, as its use in these populations has not been studied. NIASPAN is contraindicated in patients with significant or unexplained hepatic dysfunction. 20. Patients with a history of jaundice, hepatobiliary disease, or peptic ulcer should be closely monitored during NIASPAN therapy. 21. Niacin therapy can increase fasting blood glucose levels, and diabetic patients may experience a dose-related increase in glucose intolerance. Blood glucose levels should be monitored frequently, and adjustments to diet or hypoglycemic therapy may be necessary. 22. NIASPAN has been associated with small but statistically significant dose-related reductions in platelet count and increases in prothrombin time. Caution should be observed when administering NIASPAN concomitantly with anticoagulants, and platelet counts and prothrombin time should be monitored closely. 23. Elevated uric acid levels have been reported with niacin therapy, so caution is advised in patients predisposed to gout. 24. NIASPAN has been associated with small but statistically significant reductions in phosphorus levels. Periodic monitoring of phosphorus levels is recommended in patients at risk for hypophosphatemia. 25. Liver function tests should be performed on all patients during NIASPAN therapy. Serum transaminase levels, including AST and ALT, should be monitored before treatment begins, every 6 to 12 weeks for the first year, and periodically thereafter. 26. If transaminase levels rise to three times the upper limit of normal (ULN) and are persistent, or if they are associated with symptoms such as nausea, fever, or malaise, the drug should be discontinued. 27. Niacin therapy has been associated with abnormal liver tests, including elevations in serum transaminases, LDH, fasting glucose, uric acid, total bilirubin, amylase, and creatine kinase, as well as reductions in phosphorus. 28. Caution should be exercised when prescribing niacin (≥1 g/day) with statins, as this combination increases the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Combination therapy with NIASPAN and lovastatin or simvastatin should not exceed doses of 2,000 mg NIASPAN and 40 mg lovastatin or simvastatin daily. 29. Niacin may potentiate the effects of ganglionic blocking agents and vasoactive drugs, resulting in postural hypotension. Caution is advised when using niacin with antihypertensive therapy. 30. Niacin may produce false elevations in some fluorometric determinations of plasma or urinary catecholamines and false-positive reactions with Benedict’s reagent in urine glucose tests. 31. NIASPAN is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. It is not known whether niacin at doses used for lipid disorders can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. If a woman becomes pregnant while taking niacin for primary hyperlipidemia, the drug should be discontinued. 32. Niacin is excreted into human milk, but the actual infant dose is unknown. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 33. Safety and effectiveness of niacin therapy in pediatric patients (≤16 years) have not been established. 34. In clinical studies of NIASPAN, no overall differences in safety and effectiveness were observed between elderly and younger patients. However, caution is advised in elderly patients due to the increased risk of adverse effects.
